title: Short Stuff: Rube Goldberg
summary: Short Stuff episode on Rube Goldberg, the cartoonist whose name became shorthand for overly complicated contraptions. Josh and Chuck (with Speaker 2 co-discussing) cover his birth and engineering training at UC Berkeley, his brief mining-engineer job before moving to New York to draw cartoons, the "Foolish Questions" strip, his national fads such as "I'm the guy" and Boob McNutt, his invention cartoons starting in 1912 including the Simple Mosquito Exterminator, Professor Lucifer Gorgonzola Butts and the fictional "Barodic" machine, his political cartoons and 1947 Pulitzer Prize win, the family name changes after death threats, and the Mousetrap game's uncredited use of his designs.

segments.title: Opening
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Short Stuff episode and the hosts greet each other.

segments.title: What a Rube Goldberg machine is
segments.summary: The hosts explain that a Rube Goldberg machine is an overly complicated contraption for a simple task, that the term dates to 1931 in the dictionary, and that Rube Goldberg was a cartoonist. They mention the mousetrap game as an inspiration and note his style resembled R. Crumb's, and that his name is an adjective in Merriam-Webster.

segments.title: Early life and engineering career
segments.summary: Goldberg was born in San Francisco in 1883, earned an engineering degree at UC Berkeley, and spent about six months mapping water and sewer lines before quitting for New York and a cartoonist job at the New York Evening Mail. His granddaughter Jennifer George wrote a book about him.

segments.title: Three Stooges screenplay and Foolish Questions
segments.summary: The hosts note Goldberg wrote the Three Stooges movie Soup to Nuts and that he first gained fame with the Foolish Questions cartoon, of which he drew close to 450 to 500, which were sparked by reader suggestions.

segments.title: I'm the Guy trend and Boob McNutt
segments.summary: Goldberg created national trends like the I'm the Guy feature and the Boob McNutt strip, which the hosts say is less funny today but well drawn.

segments.title: Simple Mosquito Exterminator and invention cartoons
segments.summary: Goldberg began drawing his invention cartoons in 1912. The hosts read the Simple Mosquito Exterminator description, a schematic with lettered parts explained in captions.

segments.title: Professor Butts and the fictional Barodic machine
segments.summary: Professor Lucifer Gorgonzola Butts was based on two College professors, Samuel B. Christie and Frederick Slate. Goldberg described the Barodic, a convoluted machine meant to weigh the earth, which was a fictional joke; a later article examined it and found only a barometer with a similar name.

segments.title: Satire and political cartoons
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the satire of technology complicating simple processes. Goldberg was a conservative who criticized the growing federal government under FDR, won a Pulitzer for a 1947 cartoon titled Peace Today, received death threats, and the family changed their surname.

segments.title: Mousetrap royalties dispute
segments.summary: Mousetrap game reportedly used components from Goldberg's drawings without paying royalties; Marvin Glass is blamed for it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck closes with the standard Stuff You Should Know production and iHeartRadio credit.
